As mentioned, here is a verbatim copy of the extended appendix section on sub-group fairness and sub-group calibration. The previous rebuttal PDF in the global comment shows example sub-group calibration plots for Mixtral 8x22B with confidence intervals.

> This section contains additional subgroup calibration plots on the ACSIncome task.
Figure 6 shows the 2 worst offenders: Yi 34B and Mixtral 8x22B.
Figures A1 and A2 show the remaining models.
The same trend is visible but to a lesser extent: Instruction-tuned models show a bias towards lower scores for Black individuals, even after controlling for label prevalence.

> We can quantify the positive score bias by evaluating the _signed calibration error_ (SCE):
$\mathrm{SCE} := \frac{1}{n} \sum_{m=1}^M \sum_{i\in B_m} (r_i - y_i)$,
where $M$ is the number of score buckets, $B_m$ is the set of sample indices belonging to bucket $m$, $r_i = f_\theta(x_i)$ is the risk score given to sample $x_i$ and $y_i$ is its label.
This metric does not evaluate overall calibration, as a value of 0 does not indicate a calibrated classifier. Instead, negative/positive values indicate a bias towards lower/higher risk scores, respectively.
If higher scores are related to positive real-world outcomes (e.g., when predicting income for a loan application), then a bias towards lower scores on samples of specific protected subgroups would likely lead to unfair real-world outcomes.
Conversely, if a negative class prediction is associated with a positive outcome (e.g., when predicting risk of recidivism), then a bias towards lower scores would be beneficial for the affected group.

> Figure A3 shows the difference between the signed calibration error (SCE) on different group pairings, on the ACSIncome task. Positive predictions ($Y=1$) correspond to the advantaged high-income class.
Negative differences, $\Delta_{SCE} < 0$, indicates advantaged scores for Black individuals, while positive differences, $\Delta_{SCE} > 0$, indicate disadvantaged scores for Black individuals.
Interestingly, while subgroup calibration curves appear similar for base models and disadvantage Black individuals for instruction-tuned models 
(see Figures 6, A1, and A2), this is not entirely reflected on the SCE metric.
Indeed, a clear-cut split is visible: base models benefit the score of Black individuals, and instruct models disadvantage the score of Black individuals.
This finding could be partially explained by the fact that base models produce score distributions with low variance, and instruct models produce high-variance polarized outcomes.
Specifically, two conclusions can be drawn from the score distributions produced by base models: 
(1) models under-estimate the score of high-income earners (which are disproportionately Asian), and (2) models over-estimate the score of low-income earners (which are disproportionately Black).
This could lead base models to over-estimate the earnings of the Black population disproportionately to other groups.
The opposite is true for instruction-tuned models: high-income earners see their score over-estimated, which benefits groups with a higher prevalence of high earners.

> This in no way serves as an exhaustive analysis of risk score fairness on LLMs, as it is bound to be highly task dependent and language model dependent.
We simply surface the fact that, on this high-income prediction task, risk scores are not group-calibrated [Barocas et al., 2023] and could lead to unfair outcomes.
Crucially, even though race has the lowest mean feature importance among all features (see Appendix A.4), we report and explain how different trends in risk score distributions can effectively lead to unfair outcomes.

Thank you for your continued feedback and for engaging in the rebuttal

We have now **added results for a numeric prompting scheme** that directly queries the model for a numeric probability estimate instead of posing the question as a multiple-choice. With this addition, we arguably cover the two most popular prompting schemes for LLMs: either multiple-choice Q&A  [Santurkar et al., 2023; Argyle et al., 2023; Tamkin et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2024], or verbalized prompts for a direct numeric answer in token space [Tian et al., 2023]. Results for this numeric prompting scheme were added to the paper, and are shown in the Table 2 of the global comment. We have also **added results for the GPT-4o-mini model**, together with compatibility with a variety of closed-source language models available through web APIs.

Results show consistently **improved calibration across instruction-tuned models** with numeric risk prompting, but the same is not observed for base models. At the same time, we observe **small but consistent drops in predictive power** of the risk scores produced by LLMs (lower ROC AUC). This can arguably be attributed to the fact that models do not use the full 0-100 space of numeric answers, but instead often use only a few possible outputs (e.g., 10%, 25%, 50%, 75%, 90%). This discretization of risk score outputs can lead to more ties and lower discriminative power of the scores. As far as we know, this difference between base models and instruction-tuned models for different uncertainty estimation schemes has not yet been reported in related literature. Results for the remaining benchmark tasks with numeric risk prompting will be added to the paper appendix. It is noteworthy that, with numeric risk prompting, the best model (GPT-4o-mini) essentially surpasses or closely approximates a supervised linear model on all metrics, where the latter was fitted on 1.5M data samples, and the former saw no training data.

---

> Additional Experiments on Popular Dataset

As you point out, it is entirely possible to evaluate ECE on other popular Q&A datasets. However, when evaluating ECE on knowledge-testing datasets such as MMLU or GSM8K, the uncertainty expressed by the model is fully attributed to a lack of perfect knowledge by the model. In contrast, expressing uncertainty on ACS tasks is in itself a form of knowledge, as the true answer is uncertain. Risk scores relate to model uncertainty and to true data uncertainty; our goal is to evaluate how LLMs fare in settings with true data uncertainty, where a perfect model is forced to output uncertain answers.
The American Community Survey is one such data source, covering a wide range of statistics on all aspects of life of the American population. We hope to contribute further results for this evaluation on different high-quality population surveys. One such example is the medical expenditure panel survey (MEPS) dataset used in [this folktexts notebook](https://socialfoundations.github.io/folktexts/notebooks/custom-dataset-example.html), which shows similar results to the ACS tasks. More detailed results on MEPS will be added to the paper appendix.
> Limited scope

It is indeed possible and even expected that LLMs should have different levels of calibration to different real-world tasks. We provide more than 5 such tasks, and draw general trends but see some differences when predicting outcomes relating to different aspects of life. We have also now added results with a different prompting scheme for a more thorough model evaluation. We don’t claim to draw conclusions relating to LLM’s calibration in general, but instead `folktexts` should be used to evaluate LLMs in conjunction with other benchmarks for a broader evaluation of a model’s capabilities. We do believe our package serves a previously under-served direction of LLM evaluation.

> Proper level of abstraction

Thank you for pointing this out. We are aware that too much abstraction can impair code usability and create unnecessary hurdles for simpler tasks. That is precisely why we make available a [command line script `run_acs_benchmark`](https://github.com/socialfoundations/folktexts/blob/main/folktexts/cli/run_acs_benchmark.py), as well as a higher-level `folktexts.Benchmark` interface that can be used with a minimal set of arguments (at least model-name and task-name). We will strive to expose popular functionalities in these higher-level interfaces, while keeping more customized usage to the lower level classes.

---

We hope our latest paper and repository additions have effectively addressed your concerns. We see the added numeric prompting scheme as a definitive improvement to the contributions of our work. Do let us know of any remaining questions.

Thank you for your thorough feedback. The following paragraphs go through all questions and suggestions. Please let us know if your questions were addressed, or of any further questions you may have.

---
> Why create a new package that only uses ACS data? The authors could have contributed to existing LLM packages for tabular data, which support more datasets and already have an established user base.

There are two important distinctions to existing benchmarks. First, we focus on quantifying outcome uncertainty. To quantify outcome uncertainty against a ground truth we need data points sampled from a known population. Otherwise, it is unclear what we’re asking a model to do. The ACS data is carefully curated to reflect US population statistics and we can check how good a model is in reflecting uncertainty in human outcomes. The vast majority of datasets available in existing packages can not be combined with such an evaluation.

The main goal of _folktexts_ is to provide all pipeline parts that enable the use of LLMs to produce risk scores, together with a ready-to-use high-quality data source (ACS). To clarify the scope of our package, we’ve added a jupyter notebook showcasing how to use folktexts on a different dataset.

> How does the user select the variables to consider?

Variables can be selected by instantiating a `TaskMetadata` object with the target list of `features=[...]`.

We’ve added an example jupyter notebook showcasing [how to create a custom ACS task](https://socialfoundations.github.io/folktexts/notebooks/custom-acs-task-example.html).

> Can they change the instructions?

The folktexts package does not provide LLMs with any specific instructions on how to properly classify input samples. We recognize accuracy could potentially be improved by providing domain-expert instructions on how to classify each input, but the models should still be able to quantify their own uncertainty when considering an underspecified question. In the absence of instructions or domain knowledge, the model’s answers should ideally be low-confidence risk scores. Our results show that this is not the case.

> Does the package support fine-tuning of the LLM?

Our package is intended to focus on evaluation and benchmarking of existing models, not on model building. However, the folktexts pipeline can be leveraged to easily fine-tune existing models on ACS prediction tasks.

> In line 293, the authors list a set of features. The reader won't know what these features mean unless they look up the survey codebook.

Thanks for pointing this out. The feature definitions are contained in Table 2 of the supplementary materials. A reference to this table was indeed missing, and we’ve since added it to line 293.

> The points in Figure 5 are supposedly obtained by removing one feature at a time. Why are there 7 features but only 4 points? Are the authors removing features that are not sensitive attributes?

There was a bug in Figure 5 that was corrected in the supplementary materials submitted with the paper (see Appendix A). We’ve since updated the plot (see rebuttal PDF) to show 2 features removed at a time, from 10 features down to 2 (5 points per model). This is less cluttered and easier to interpret.

> The authors should provide suggestions on how to add support for models from providers like OpenAI, Anthropic, and others. These models are used in most academic papers. 

It would be ideal to include support for closed-source models available through an API. However, most of these models do not allow access to the output token log-probabilities, which is required to extract continuous risk scores instead of a discrete output answer. As such, we do not think it currently makes sense to attempt to integrate closed-source models with a process that requires access to internal log-probabilities.

> Lines in Figure 4 should include confidence intervals.

You’re right, thanks for pointing this out. We’ve now added 95% confidence intervals to Figure 4 as well as other calibration curves ([see example here](https://github.com/socialfoundations/folktexts/blob/main/results/imgs/calibration-curves-per-subgroup.Mixtral-8x22B-v0.1.pdf) or in the rebuttal PDF).

We agree, and thank you for the suggestion. An FAQ section has been added to the [README](https://github.com/socialfoundations/folktexts?tab=readme-ov-file#faq), and several new example notebooks have been added to the github repository.

> Discussion of prior work could be improved.

Thank you for the reference papers. We’ve extended related work discussion, including discussion of related work on using LLMs for tabular data predictions [Slack and Singh, 2023; Hegselmann et al, 2023], and a discussion on fairness assessment of LLMs on tabular data [Tamkin et al, 2023; Liu et al, 2024].

> Other packages could be cited, such as Tablet.

Thank you for this reference. We’ve included it in the related work section. However, we’d like to clarify that the `Tablet` package has an entirely different focus: quantifying how in-context task instructions change the performance of LLMs on tabular data, disregarding uncertainty quantification.

> Package documentation needs to be improved.

To address this concern, we have now included three additional jupyter notebooks with example usages of our package ([see live notebook examples here](https://socialfoundations.github.io/folktexts/notebooks.html)), we have included an FAQ section as per your suggestion, and created a live website with code documentation and showcasing example usages of our package.

We appreciate your insightful comments and the opportunity to address them. Let us first clarify the intended use, and the unique selling point of our package before we go through individual questions.

The intended use of our package is as an evaluation tool, complementing existing metrics along which to evaluate a new language model. We are not aware of any existing calibration toolbox that offers non-realizable prediction tasks for evaluating risk scores. The deviation from yes/no questions is essential for evaluating uncertainty quantification. For example, on benchmarks where there is a single correct answer to every question, a model does not need to express uncertainty to be accurate (a model that outputs answers with 100% confidence can be accurate and calibrated). However, it will be unclear whether the same model can express the inherent uncertainty on unrealizable prediction tasks where there is no single correct answer; in this case, models are forced to express uncertainty, and an accurate and calibrated model should output lower confidence scores. Our results show that all instruction-tuned models fail to do this, but instead continue outputting high confidence answers regardless of ground-truth uncertainty. This reveals a common failure point that would not be detectable on standard benchmarks: over-confident answers even in the presence of real-world uncertainty. This is an important caveat to the use of LLMs in the context of risk assessment on human subjects, where there is rarely a certain outcome. Thus our results provide new insights, in addition to confirming existing literature results.

---

> The dataset used for calibration evaluation is flexible but covers a limited domain with fixed-structure questions. [...] it would be valuable to see systematic evaluations on other popular QA datasets. 

Most popular Q&A datasets do not feature any data uncertainty, i.e., there is a single correct answer to each question on MMLU, GSM8K, etc. Conversely, the prediction tasks we formulate often have no exact answer, forcing models to show uncertainty to have accurate responses.

Thus, instead of expanding along the axis of data sources, our focus has been on varying tasks on this data. Each attribute in the dataset offers a different task with a different level of outcome uncertainty; and we can vary which features to include in the prediction task to controllably increase/decrease uncertainty. We have now added results on four additional ACS PUMS tasks, relating to travel time prediction, health insurance coverage prediction, prediction of address changes among young adults, and employment prediction. These tasks follow popular tabular benchmarks introduced by Ding et al. (2021). Additional tasks can be easily created from the same data source: we’ve now added a jupyter notebook detailing how to create custom tasks (see global comment for links to all added notebooks). We’ve also added a notebook showcasing the use of `folktexts` on the MEPS dataset.

> Numerous methods have been proposed for estimating prediction confidence in large language models, and the package would benefit from a more inclusive approach to have at least some of them implemented.

We mainly focused on log-probabilities because of its popular use in the context of survey evaluations [e.g., Santurkar et al, 2023; Argyle et al, 2023]. We recognize that another option is for the model to output a textual answer that reflects its uncertainty, instead of having calibrated internal logodds, as used by related work on uncertainty quantification [e.g., Tian et al, 2023]. We agree that results with a different uncertainty quantification method would be valuable to our package and our paper. _As such, we aim to add these results in the following week, and undoubtedly before the rebuttal deadline of September 1st_. Additionally, we wanna point out that adding a new method to quantify uncertainty of LLM answers can be easily achieved by implementing a sub-class of 
`QAInterface`.

> Given the existence of useful and efficient packages for each component along this pipeline (...)

We make extensive use of known open-source dependencies throughout our package, when they are available. Still, the code-base spans 5K lines of code connecting such components (without counting notebooks or tests). As far as we know, no open-source package provides this functionality in one easy-to-use package. Related packages focus on discrete answers (not risk scores), often on realizable tasks, where there is a fixed question and a single correct answer. We provide a malleable set of classes, together with a suite of benchmark tasks with inherent uncertainty, intended to evaluate models on a previously under-explored axis.

> Overall, it is clear what the package is intended to achieve, but the intended scope and usage are not sufficiently discussed in the paper.

We are happy to work this rebuttal discussion into the paper to clarify its intended use. Besides the paper, we believe other ML artifacts such as the package documentation and open-source code-base are key to clarify scope and intended usage of the package. We have now greatly improved package documentation, including a range of example usage notebooks. Orthogonally, the paper is intended to contextualize the project and contribute a plethora of interesting initial insights regarding calibration of current LLMs, raising this miscalibration issue to the ML community.

> _Minor:_ In Figure 1, the two choices do not appear to be mutually exclusive. Why should that be the case?

Thanks for pointing this out. There was a typo on the answer prompt. It’s now been corrected to “$50,000”.

Thank you for your feedback.

Let us emphasize that we contribute a package for LLM evaluation. Our focus is not to build models. Thus, questions related to fine-tuning and calibration techniques are orthogonal to our work. Folktexts offers a framework to systematically extract risk scores from an LLM and benchmark these risk scores against human population statistics. The object to evaluate is a given LLM. As such our package can be applied to any model, for example, to evaluate how it performs pre/post fine-tuning or what the gain of a new calibration technique is, but proposing better models is outside the scope of this work.

The following paragraphs address each raised question and suggestion.

> **Expand Evaluation Metrics and Integrate Fairness Evaluation**

Folktexts extracts risk scores. Thus, any evaluation metric that takes as input $(X,Y)$ and a risk score $R$ can be easily added to the package. It’s also compatible with any existing fairness evaluation package that takes $(Y,S,R)$ as input, where $S$ is the sensitive attributes. This way, folktexts bridges the gap between evaluating LLMs and standard evaluation of ML classifiers, making it possible to use any standard ML evaluation package to evaluate LLMs out-of-the-box.

The full list of metrics currently available through folktexts is: accuracy, ROC AUC, ECE, quantiled ECE, log-loss, Brier score, precision, TPR/FPR/FNR/TNR, positive-prediction rate, as well as fairness metrics such as equalized odds, equal opportunity, and predictive equality. Additionally, a variety of plots is automatically outputted by folktexts, including sub-group specific calibration curves to audit fairness of risk scores.


> **Limited Calibration Performance: (...) results indicate significant miscalibration**

The fact that we find significant miscalibration among state-of-the-art LLMs arguably does not constitute a limitation but a strong contribution of our work. We provide a package for model evaluation, not model building. Our package could indeed be used to test the effectiveness of calibration techniques, by evaluating LLMs pre and post calibration interventions.


> **Real world constraints**

As you point out, calibration alone is not sufficient as a criteria to assess the real world impact of models. We are very explicit about this in the paper, and note that the same is true for a benchmark that only focuses on accuracy as a metric. But any additional axis we have available along which to evaluate models can help mitigate the risk after deployment. The axis we offer is calibration on unrealizable prediction tasks. This is an axis that has not been studied before. 


> **Narrow scope**

The focus on American Community Survey (ACS) data is intentional. The ACS offers a high-quality, well curated data source, as well as a code book for how questions have been framed when gathering the data. This data can be used to derive multiple prediction tasks, representing different aspects of society (income, address mobility, commute time, etc.), and how they evolve over the years the survey was conducted.


> **Provide more information regarding experiments, to make paper reproducible**

All code required to run our experiments is not only open-source but also easily runnable from the command line as described in the 
[github repository](https://github.com/socialfoundations/folktexts?tab=readme-ov-file#basic-setup). Additionally, all results are made available in [CSV format](https://github.com/socialfoundations/folktexts/tree/main/results) and notebooks to generate paper plots are also 
[made available](https://github.com/socialfoundations/folktexts/tree/main/notebooks).

We believe we have abided by the utmost standards for reproducibility. Please let us know of any missing ML artifacts.

Thank you for the feedback. We address each question in the following paragraphs. Please let us know if anything remains unclear.

---

**Q1**

> L262: what are base-model counterparts? Is it the QA without the first two steps in prompting LLMs in Sec 3.2?

We use the term “base-model counterpart” for the version of the same LLM without instruction-tuning. For example, the `Meta-Llama-3-70B` is the _base-model counterpart_ or _base-model variant_ of the `Meta-Llama-3-70B-Instruct` model. We’ve added a clarifying sentence to the paper.

**Q2**

> L263: "without access to any task-related data". The prompts are accessible to the models; are they not task-related?

Yes, the prompts are the only data each model receives to compute the zero-shot risk score. This sentence was meant to highlight that no “training data” exists, and these risk scores could be computed without any data besides the information regarding the current individual. We’ve updated this sentence to “without access to any _prior_ task-related data”.

**Q3**

> L266: "While ROC is agnostic to calibration, accuracy on the maximum likelihood answer is not.". I get it that for thresholded classifiers, AUC doesn't depend on the threshold, but accuracy does. But why AUC is high whereas accuracy is worse than random guess? This is curious especially for the class balanced case. AUC is high means the two populations are well separated, and no matter what threshold is chosen, the error probability (sum of the areas of the smaller bump on the two sides of the threshold) should be larger than 0.5.

Thank you for bringing up this question.

Regardless of how strong ROC AUC performance is, every ROC curve necessarily includes two points that correspond to constant classifiers: the bottom-left point corresponds to always predicting the negative class, and the top-right point corresponds to always predicting the positive class. On a calibrated model, the $\tau=0.5$ threshold would maximize accuracy. On the other hand, if the score distribution is too extreme (as is the example of the `gemma` family of models), all predicted scores could lie above/below the 0.5 threshold. Such LLMs would essentially always output the same answer regardless of the input prompt (when generating text using the argmax token). Our results show that, despite the text outputs of such constant-answer LLMs being essentially worthless for predictions, their internal risk scores are still highly predictive. By calibrating the binarization threshold $\tau$ we can extract useful binary predictions out of these extreme score distributions, as shown by the right-most column of Table 1.

As you point out, in the case of a balanced class distribution, any ROC point above the diagonal would lead to an expected accuracy larger than or equal to $0.50$. However, on our benchmark datasets, the classes are not perfectly balanced. In the case of the income prediction task, the base rate is $P[Y=1] = 0.39$. Therefore, even though a random classifier achieves an expected accuracy of $0.50$, a classifier that constantly predicts the positive class achieves $0.39$ accuracy. This is exactly why multiple models achieve this value of accuracy even though their ROC AUC is significantly higher than a random classifier, i.e., because all risk scores produced by such LLMs lie above the $0.50$ threshold.

We’ve added a sentence clarifying this situation, and stating that the classes are not balanced.



**Suggestions and minor issues**

> The data points in Figure 5 exhibit high noise variance. For ECE, it is known that it underestimates the calibration error and the value is sensitive to the bin number [1]. One choice is to use $B=\Theta(n^{1/3})$ in quantile-based measure of ECE to achieve the minimum bias [2].

Thank you for the references. Note that there was a bug on the values of Figure 5 that was promptly corrected in the supplementary materials submitted one week later (the submitted PDF contains the corrected plot). The true values do not exhibit such high noise variance, and show a more interesting trend: providing more information leads to higher ROC AUC, but generally worsens calibration for base models. The rebuttal PDF published in the global comment contains the [updated plot](https://github.com/socialfoundations/folktexts/blob/main/results/imgs/feature-ablation.Meta-Llama-3-8B.Meta-Llama-3-70B.Mistral-7B-v0.1.Mixtral-8x7B-v0.1.Mixtral-8x22B-v0.1.pdf).

> - For Figure 4, I think the left is instruction tuned model and the right is base model based on the score distribution in Figure 3.
> - The fonts in the Figure 3,4,5 are too small compared to the main text.
> - L188: AGER, vs Figure 1: AREG
> - L188: Infromation -> Information

Thank you for pointing these out. We’ve corrected the caption of Figure 4 (the titles are correct but the captions have been swapped), corrected typos, and increased the fontsize of all plots for better readability.

---
Thank you once again for your suggestions and feedback. As a result of reviewer feedback, we’ve made several paper updates, and greatly improved package documentation (changes summarized in the global comment). Please let us know if anything remains unclear regarding our contributions.

review.value:
1. Enhanced Calibration Techniques:

- How do you plan to develop and incorporate advanced calibration techniques to better align model predictions with actual outcomes, particularly for instruction-tuned models?
- What specific calibration methods do you believe would be most effective in improving the miscalibration observed in the evaluated models?

2. Expand Evaluation Metrics:

- Are there plans to introduce additional uncertainty quantification methods, such as confidence intervals or conformal prediction methods, to provide a more complete picture of model performance?
- How do you plan to ensure that these additional metrics will be integrated into the existing folktexts framework?

- Do you have any plans to integrate folktexts with existing fairness evaluation efforts to ensure that calibration improvements also translate to fair and equitable model performance across different population groups?
- How do you propose to address the potential for calibration metrics to misrepresent fairness and accuracy in certain contexts?

4. Evaluation of Real-World Applications:

- Given that calibration metrics alone are not sufficient criteria for consequential risk assessment applications, how do you propose to evaluate the real-world impact of your calibrated models?
- What additional measures or metrics do you believe are necessary to ensure that the models are both calibrated and practically useful in real-world applications?

5. Instruction-Tuning Processes:

- Your results indicate that instruction-tuned models often show worse calibration. What changes or improvements do you propose to the current instruction-tuning processes to address this issue?
- Have you identified any specific aspects of the instruction-tuning process that contribute to miscalibration, and if so, how do you plan to address them?

1. Comprehensive Calibration Evaluation:
The paper introduces "folktexts," a software package specifically designed to evaluate and benchmark the calibration properties of large language models (LLMs). This is a significant contribution as calibration is crucial for assessing the uncertainty in model predictions.

2. Versatile and User-Friendly:
Folktexts features an easy-to-use and extensible API, allowing researchers to evaluate different models, metrics, prompting templates, and ways to extract predictive scores. This flexibility is crucial for comprehensive evaluation and benchmarking.
The package includes pre-specified natural language benchmark tasks that can be used with any HuggingFace transformer model, making it accessible and practical for the research community.
3. Large-Scale Evaluation:
The paper demonstrates the utility of folktexts through a large-scale evaluation of 14 popular LLMs, showing strong predictive capabilities but highlighting significant calibration issues.
The evaluation covers various models, including instruction-tuned variants, providing a broad perspective on the current state of LLM calibration.
4. Focus on Subgroup Calibration:
Folktexts allows for subgroup calibration evaluation, which is important for assessing algorithmic fairness and ensuring that models perform consistently across different population segments.
The paper provides empirical findings on the calibration curves for different subpopulations, emphasizing the need for detailed inspection of model performance across groups.

opportunities_for_improvement.value:
1. Calibration Versus Volume:
While the package effectively measures calibration, the paper acknowledges that many LLMs are miscalibrated despite their strong predictive signal. This highlights a gap in the current ability to develop well-calibrated models.
The results indicate that instruction-tuned models often show worse calibration, suggesting that current tuning processes might not prioritize or effectively address calibration. Can you explain this in a better way? Is there any reasonable explanation? Why is this happening? Intuitively fine-tuned models should work better than the ones that are not fine-tuned.
2.Lack of Comprehensive Technical Details:
The paper could provide more detailed information on the preprocessing steps, error analysis, and computational resources used. This would improve reproducibility and allow for more precise comparisons. Provide more information regarding experiments, to make paper reproducible.
3. Potential for Misinterpretation:
Calibration metrics alone may not be sufficient criteria for using LLMs in consequential risk assessment applications. The paper notes that a calibrated model does not necessarily ensure fairness or accuracy in all contexts, which could lead to misinterpretation of the results. Is there any way to improve this by providing additional metrics?

limitations.value:
1. Limited Calibration Performance:
Despite the strong predictive capabilities of the evaluated models, the results indicate significant miscalibration, particularly in instruction-tuned models. This highlights the need for improved calibration techniques that are not yet addressed by the current package.
Technical Documentation Gaps:

2.Focus on Calibration Metrics:
The evaluation focuses primarily on calibration metrics, which, while important, are not sufficient criteria for assessing the full utility of models in real-world applications. Calibration alone does not guarantee that the models are suitable for consequential risk assessment tasks.

3. Insufficient Fairness Analysis:
While subgroup calibration is evaluated, the paper does not fully integrate fairness evaluation efforts. This could limit the understanding of how calibration improvements impact different population segments and whether they ensure equitable model performance.

4. Instruction-Tuning Issues:
The results indicate that instruction-tuned models often exhibit worse calibration than their base counterparts. The paper does not provide a detailed analysis of why this occurs or how to mitigate this issue, leaving a gap in understanding the impact of instruction-tuning on model calibration.

5. Real-World Application Constraints:
The paper does not provide sufficient criteria for evaluating the real-world impact of calibrated models. Calibration metrics alone do not address the broader implications and potential risks of deploying these models in practical, high-stakes scenarios.

6. Narrow Scope of Evaluation:
The empirical evaluation is limited to specific tasks derived from the American Community Survey. While this provides valuable insights, the scope of evaluation could be broadened to include other datasets and prediction tasks to generalize the findings.

summary_and_contributions.value: This paper introduces folktexts, a software package designed to provide datasets derived from US Census data and tools to evaluate and benchmark the calibration of LLMs on these datasets. The evaluation follows a prompting QA setting, where the log probabilities for positive and negative answers are extracted to compute the scoring function, and calibration is measured using the Expected Calibration Error. This evaluation scheme is then applied to multiple language models, both before and after instruction fine-tuning.

review.value:
This paper is clearly written, and I appreciate the thorough analysis conducted by the author and the clarifications provided throughout the text regarding "calibration vs. accuracy" and "similar calibration curves vs. fairness." However, I find the scope somewhat limited, and some design choices are introduced without clear justification.

For instance, it seems to me that the use of PUMS data allows for direct evaluation of instance-level calibration error against the ground truth distribution label. If that is the case, further justification is needed for selecting ECE as the empirical metric, especially given the known binning problem discussed by the authors.

Additionally, the paper includes a detailed discussion on model calibration but lacks an explanation for favoring the probability ratio in language generation and QA tasks. Numerous methods have been proposed for estimating prediction confidence in large language models, and the package would benefit from a more inclusive approach to have at least some of them implemented. While this package offers a degree of customizability, I found the pre-implemented options to be somewhat rigid and limited. Additionally, it is unclear what this passage aims to abstract beyond various packages for prompting LLMs through APIs, efficient queries for local LLMs, or even calibration evaluation and plotting.

Another concern is the generalizability of the evaluation results. The dataset used for calibration evaluation is flexible but covers a limited domain with fixed-structure questions. If ECE is adopted as the evaluation metric, it would be valuable to see systematic evaluations on other popular QA datasets. Addressing this and including more evaluation configurations would significantly enhance the package.

strengths.value: This paper provides clear background information and includes careful discussions that prevent overclaiming and incorrect interpretations. It introduces a straightforward method to derive calibration tasks from structured data, potentially enabling more comprehensive calibration evaluations. The analysis of LLM calibration is insightful, with several findings aligning with known results, thereby adding validity to their observations.

opportunities_for_improvement.value: As discussed above, the primary area for improvement is the limited scope of results included in the paper and the pre-implemented solutions in the package. Given the existence of useful and efficient packages for each component along this pipeline, the major contribution of a package like this would be to provide a carefully curated list of methods and datasets that can be easily adopted and verified. Currently, this aspect is somewhat lacking in the presented work.

limitations.value: The authors provide a well-considered discussion on the limitations of using calibration as a fairness metric and correctly address the scope of their work. A minor suggestion would be to also discuss the limitations in the scope of the evaluation, which aligns with my previous points.

correctness.value: I find the claims in the paper to be carefully considered and reasonably supported.

clarity.value: A minor question: In Figure 1, the two choices do not appear to be mutually exclusive. Why should that be the case?

relation_to_prior_work.value: This paper discusses many prior works on LLM calibration evaluation. However, it could benefit from expanding and discussing some of the conclusions from previous works. For example, including comparisons of in-domain vs. out-domain data, structured vs. unstructured data, threshold selection, with and without instruction tuning, and multiple pass self-consistency. This would help better position the work and justify some of the design choices in the default implementation.

documentation.value: Overall, it is clear what the package is intended to achieve, but the intended scope and usage are not sufficiently discussed in the paper. Additionally, the package does not appear to be adequately documented, even with Appendix C. For example, it is unclear what kinds of risk estimation pipelines are included in the package, how the output is intended to be interpreted, and what the advantages are of using this package instead of implementing solutions from scratch.

title.value: The paper introduces folktexts, a package for benchmarking the calibration of LLM on tabular prediction tasks on Census data

summary_and_contributions.value: The paper introduces folktexts, a software package designed to evaluate the calibration of LLMs using datasets derived from the American Community Survey (ACS). These datasets are obtained leveraging the popular folktables. The package features an extensible API for testing various models, metrics, and prompting strategies. Empirical results demonstrate that while LLMs show strong predictive abilities, their outputs are often miscalibrated.

review.value: Overall, the paper is clear and the package is likely to be useful to the community. The empirical analysis effectively demonstrates the potential uses of the package. However, the package needs clearer documentation, support for fine-tuning, and compatibility with more models.

strengths.value: The package will be valuable to the growing community of researchers working on LLMs for tabular predictive tasks. The paper is well-written and easy to understand, providing clear explanations of the methodology and the tools included in the folktexts package. The evaluation effectively demonstrates the package's potential, revealing significant calibration issues in popular LLMs. Additionally, the package opens up opportunities for further interesting studies, such as examining miscalibration over time.

opportunities_for_improvement.value:
### Questions
* Why create a new package that only uses ACS data? The authors could have contributed to existing LLM packages for tabular data, which support more datasets and already have an established user base.
* How does the user select the variables to consider? Can they change the instructions?
* Does the package support fine-tuning of the LLM?
* In line 293, the authors list a set of features. The reader won't know what these features mean unless they look up the survey codebook.
* The points in Figure 5 are supposedly obtained by removing one feature at a time. Why are there 7 features but only 4 points? Are the authors removing features that are not sensitive attributes?

### Suggestions
* The authors should provide suggestions on how to add support for models from providers like OpenAI, Anthropic, and others. These models are used in most academic papers. 
* Lines in Figure 4 should include confidence intervals.
* It would be useful if the authors answered these questions in the README or elsewhere.
* Other packages could be cited, such as [Tablet](https://github.com/dylan-slack/Tablet).

relation_to_prior_work.value: Discussion of prior work could be improved. There is existing research on applying LLMs to tabular data and examining their fairness properties. This [survey paper](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2402.17944) summarizes many recent advances.

documentation.value: Package documentation needs to be improved.

title.value: Evaluating language models as risk scores

abstract.value:
Current question-answering benchmarks predominantly focus on accuracy in realizable prediction tasks.
Conditioned on a question and answer-key, does the most likely token match the ground truth?
Such benchmarks necessarily fail to evaluate LLMs' ability to quantify ground-truth outcome uncertainty.
In this work, we focus on the use of LLMs as risk scores for unrealizable prediction tasks.
We introduce folktexts, a software package to systematically generate risk scores using LLMs, and evaluate them against US Census data products.
A flexible API enables the use of different prompting schemes, local or web-hosted models, and diverse census columns that can be used to compose custom prediction tasks.
We evaluate 17 recent LLMs across five proposed benchmark tasks.
We find that zero-shot risk scores produced by multiple-choice question-answering have high predictive signal but are widely miscalibrated.
Base models consistently overestimate outcome uncertainty, while instruction-tuned models underestimate uncertainty and produce over-confident risk scores.
In fact, instruction-tuning polarizes answer distribution regardless of true underlying data uncertainty.
This reveals a general inability of instruction-tuned models to express data uncertainty using multiple-choice answers.
A separate experiment using verbalized chat-style risk queries yields substantially improved calibration across instruction-tuned models.
These differences in ability to quantify data uncertainty cannot be revealed in realizable settings, and highlight a blind-spot in the current evaluation ecosystem that folktexts covers.

def process(client, invitation):

    domain = client.get_group(invitation.domain)
    venue_id = domain.id
    submission_venue_id = domain.content['submission_venue_id']['value']
    venue_name = domain.content['title']['value']

    now = openreview.tools.datetime_millis(datetime.datetime.utcnow())
    cdate = invitation.cdate

    if cdate > now:
        ## invitation is in the future, do not process
        print('invitation is not yet active', cdate)
        return

    def post_submission_edit(submission):

        updated_note = openreview.api.Note(
            id=submission.id
        )

        if invitation.edit['note']['readers'] == ['everyone'] and submission.odate is None:
            updated_note.odate = now
            updated_note.content = {
                '_bibtex': {
                    'value': openreview.tools.generate_bibtex(
                        note=submission,
                        venue_fullname=venue_name,
                        year=str(datetime.datetime.utcnow().year),
                        url_forum=submission.forum,
                        paper_status='under review',
                        anonymous='readers' in submission.content['authors'] or 'readers' in invitation.edit.get('note', {}).get('content', {}).get('authors', {})
                    )
                }
            }

        client.post_note_edit(
            invitation=invitation.id,
            note=updated_note,
            signatures=[venue_id]
        )
    
    ## Release the submissions to specified readers if venueid is still submission
    submissions = client.get_all_notes(content= { 'venueid': submission_venue_id })
    print(f'update {len(submissions)} submissions')
    openreview.tools.concurrent_requests(post_submission_edit, submissions, desc='post_submission_edit')
